rv.q: The play builds to a finale that verges on rapture.
It's still a compelling play, worth seeing in itself and as a map of what would follow.
The observational clarity of Mr. Hunter's writing never falters.
This is realism pitched to an unsettling extreme, a mundanity that starts to overwhelm us even before the play gets going.
The ensemble cast is excellent and makes this a riveting piece of theater.

The quality of the writing, the vibrant coloring of the characters, and the stark originality of the playwright’s chosen milieu are already apparent, elements which make Boise well worth a Signature visit.
Butler's production is characteristically smart. The staging is always telling us more about the characters than they're saying verbally.
'A Bright New Boise' may not be his finest work, but visiting Hunter's Idaho always has its fair share of pleasures and revelations to make the trip worthwhile.
Even though the play doesn't fully succeed, those dramatic hallmarks make it worthwhile.
In 'A Bright New Boise,' the seeds are planted, but its young writer hasn't really gotten there yet.
"A Bright New Boise" takes on a subject — religious extremism — for which the playwright's gentle, oblique approach now feels insufficient.

Hunter’s characters do little else but talk about Him and religion and the rapture. Or to put it another way, they not only question how it’s all going to end, they also yammer on about the meaning of life if there is no God.
Hunter leaves the audience appreciating the play's many parts but unsure of its whole.

Under Oliver Butler's skillful direction, with a strong ensemble and remarkable lead performance by Peter Mark Kendall, Hunter's characters engage in a desperate search for meaning in ways funny, painful, and devastating.
In the sense that anything by this playwright deserves to be seen, recommending 'A Bright New Boise' will not send anyone down the wrong path, flaws and all.
Hunter takes a risk that falls short.
